members.canonical_target: The ongoing mechanisms and practices by which ensemble players keep intonation aligned during performance despite differing rates of instrument drift, i.e., how continuous adjustment is coordinated after the initial reference tuning.

The real-time mechanisms and processes by which performers modify pitch during playing to accommodate shifting harmonic contexts — i.e., how the adjustment is accomplished (perceptual feedback, technique, coordination), not merely that intonation varies.

The in-performance techniques and coordination processes by which ensemble players continuously adjust and reconcile intonation as harmonic and other contextual demands pull pitches away from the initial shared reference.

The mechanisms or practices by which ensemble players sustain accurate intonation during performance once the initial reference tone has ceased sounding — i.e., what they rely on and adjust to in place of the audible anchor.
The ongoing mechanisms or practices by which ensemble players keep pitches aligned during performance despite divergent per-instrument tendencies, rather than the initial tuning procedure.

The means or processes by which players sustain mutual intonation agreement after the initial reference tone stops sounding — i.e., what they listen to and adjust against in the absence of an external reference.

The perceptual or judgmental criterion players use to determine that a pitch match is sufficiently close to begin—i.e., how closeness to the reference is detected and what counts as adequate alignment.

The perceptual or judgment criteria musicians use to decide that intonation alignment is sufficient — i.e., what counts as 'close enough' and how that sufficiency judgment is made during tuning and play.
The perceptual criteria or cues by which players judge that pitch alignment with other ensemble members is adequate during tuning and performance.
The perceptual or judgment criteria players use to determine that pitch alignment is close enough to begin — i.e., what cues or standard signal 'sufficient' alignment.
The perceptual or practical criterion players use to judge that a pitch match is sufficiently close to stop adjusting and begin playing.
The perceptual criterion or cue players use to judge that their pitch is sufficiently aligned with the reference — i.e., what signals 'close enough' during tuning.
The perceptual cues and criteria players use to judge that their intonation adjustments have reached sufficient agreement with the ensemble.

The perceptual or judgmental criteria ensemble players use to determine that an intonation adjustment has achieved sufficient alignment — i.e., what cues or standards signal 'in tune enough' during tuning and performance.
The perceptual criteria or cues players use to judge that pitch alignment is close enough to start playing together.
The perceptual/judgment criteria and cues ensemble players use to decide that their pitch match to the reference is sufficiently close to start playing.

A ranking or identification of which specific coordination demands (momentum, balance, or timing) are most frequently degraded or fail to be preserved under marking compared to full-out dancing.
